extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for analyzing the import and kinds of propositions: what propositions assert (the exhaustive five kinds of matters of fact), distinctions between verbal/essential and real/accidental propositions, and methods for transforming abstract predicates into concrete assertions grounded on facts or phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five-fold classification of matters of fact
rubrics_metrics.description: Existence, Coexistence (Order in Place), Sequence (Order in Time), Causation, and Resemblance are the five kinds of matters of fact asserted (or denied) in every non-verbal proposition; this five-fold division is exhaustive of all matters of fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these five categories to analyze what any given proposition actually affirms or denies. Note that 'Coexistence' and 'Sequence' may be rendered as 'Order in Place' and 'Order in Time' for greater particularity; simultaneousness may be classed with Sequence under Order in Time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predicating a class-name affirms resemblance, not absolute possession
rubrics_metrics.description: When the predicate is a name of a class (a general name), predicating it often affirms merely resemblance to that class rather than absolute possession of all properties connoted by the class-name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an object lies near the boundary of a class and lacks many characteristic properties, saying the class-name of it affirms resemblance and nothing more. When uncertainty exists, qualify the predication with phrases like 'is considered' or 'may be ranked as' rather than asserting positive membership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classes based on unanalyzable resemblance (simple sensations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some classes (e.g., sensations like 'white' or feelings like 'tightness') are founded on general unanalyzable resemblance rather than analyzable shared attributes; predicating such names affirms mere likeness to past sensations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When predicates denote simple sensations or feelings, the information conveyed is just resemblance to previous sensations that bear the same name; treat these as connotative class-names expressing similarity in kind, possibly differing in degree.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract-term propositions reducible to concrete equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: Propositions whose terms are abstract can be transformed into precisely equivalent propositions in which the terms are concrete (the concrete names that connote the attributes or the names of the facts/phenomena grounding those attributes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To analyze an abstract proposition, substitute corresponding concrete terms (e.g., transform 'Thoughtlessness is dangerous' into 'Thoughtless actions are dangerous'). This reveals whether the asserted matter of fact is Existence, Coexistence, Causation, Sequence, or Resemblance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential (verbal) vs accidental (real) propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Essential (or verbal) propositions relate to the meaning of names and assert only what is involved in calling a thing by that name; accidental (non-essential) propositions—called real propositions—predicate attributes not connoted by the subject and thus can convey factual information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat essential propositions as concerned with usage/convention rather than matters of fact; they are not strictly susceptible of truth/falsity except as conformity to usage. Real propositions, by contrast, are the proper objects of proof because they add to our knowledge about things beyond mere definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions should unfold connotation to be complete
rubrics_metrics.description: A complete definition should unfold the whole of what a connotative name signifies (its entire connotation); commonly definitions specify enough to mark out the usual denotation from other known objects, sometimes using accidental properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer definitions that state the essential connotation when possible; recognize that in practice partial (practical) definitions often suffice to distinguish the intended referents from others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analysis of attribute-predication into underlying facts/phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: When a proposition predicates an attribute (e.g., 'Prudence is a virtue'), the claim can and should be analyzed into assertions about the facts or phenomena that ground that attribute (e.g., prudent persons or prudential conduct and the mental states that constitute prudence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify whether the antecedent of the asserted sequence/causation is the person, the conduct, or deeper states (e.g., 'correct foresight of consequences' as the real antecedent). Transforming the attribute-claim into grounded factual claims clarifies the kind of matter-of-fact asserted (sequence, causation, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal and particular affirmations/negations analyzed by type of matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Universal negatives and particulars are to be understood in terms of the five matters of fact: e.g., 'No horses are web-footed' denies coexistence of horse-attributes with web-feet; 'Some birds are web-footed' affirms that coexistence sometimes occurs; 'Some birds are not web-footed' asserts exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the five-fold framework to interpret universal/particular propositions: determine which of existence/coexistence/sequence/causation/resemblance is being affirmed or denied, and render the proposition in terms of the relevant facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copula ambiguity and implied existence
rubrics_metrics.description: The copula (the verb of predication) in language is ambiguous: besides marking assertion, it is a concrete word connoting existence; this gives rise to a tacit assumption of real existence in essential propositions, and accidental propositions imply the real existence of their subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that essential propositions do not really imply existence unless the speaker tacitly assumes it; non‑essential (accidental) propositions require the real existence of the subject for their meaning, so check whether existence is being presupposed when analyzing claims or proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verbal propositions are susceptible only to proof of usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Since names and their significations are arbitrary, propositions about the signification of words are not strictly true or false but conform or not to convention; the only proof they admit is proof of usage (i.e., that words have been employed by others in the intended acceptation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat verbal/essential propositions as empirical matters to be proved by facts about the world; instead, establish whether they match prevailing linguistic usage. Reserve substantive proof methods for real propositions that concern matters of fact.
